read.sections.0.text.source: Ban Chiang is a village in northeast Thailand. Under it is a low hill, or mound, built up by people who lived there long ago. Archaeologists have found pottery, graves and metal objects there. UNESCO says the people of Ban Chiang farmed rice and knew how to make bronze, a metal, very early. These people left no writing, so objects are our main clues. A pot is an artefact: an object that people made or used. We can observe its shape and its painted marks. We cannot see what its maker thought, or every way people used it.
read.sections.0.text.back: Ban Chiang is a village in north-eastern Thailand. Under the village is a low mound of earth that slowly rose from people who lived there long ago. Archaeologists found pottery, graves and objects made of metal there. UNESCO says people at Ban Chiang grew rice and knew how to make bronze, a kind of metal, from very early times. These people did not leave writing, so objects are our main clues. A pot is an artefact: a thing people made or used. We can observe the pot's shape and the painted pattern, but we cannot see what the potter was thinking, or all the things people used this pot for.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Ban Chiang is a village in Thailand. Under it is a low hill of earth. People lived there long ago. Archaeologists found pots, graves and metal things there. The people grew rice. They made bronze, a kind of metal. They left no writing. So objects are our clues. A pot is an artefact. People made it and used it. We can see its shape. We cannot see what the maker thought.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Ban Chiang is a village in Thailand. Under the village is a low mound of earth. People lived there long ago. Archaeologists found pots, graves and things made of metal. People there grew rice. They could make bronze. Bronze is a kind of metal. They did not leave writing. So objects are our clues. A pot is an artefact. People made pots and used pots. We can see the pot's shape, but we cannot see what the maker thought.

read.sections.1.text.source: In 1974 and 1975, the Penn Museum in the United States and Thailand's Fine Arts Department dug at Ban Chiang. This careful digging and recording is called an excavation. The team recorded each find's context: where it lay in the ground and what was near it. Artists drew plans, which look down on the site, and sections, which show the layers from the side. Ban Chiang was a village and also a burial place. The layers were not always neat, and one layer could hold signs of both. So a pot found in a grave raises different questions from a pot found near a house.
read.sections.1.text.back: In 1974 and 1975, the Penn Museum in the United States and Thailand's Fine Arts Department dug at Ban Chiang. Careful digging and recording like this is called excavation. The team recorded the context of each find: where it was in the ground and what was near it. Artists drew plans, which are pictures looking down from above, and drew sections, which show soil layers from the side. Ban Chiang was both a village and a burial place. The layers are not always neat, and one layer may have traces of both. So a pot found in a grave raises different questions from a pot found near a house.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: In 1974 and 1975, teams from Thailand and the United States dug at Ban Chiang. This careful digging is called an excavation. The teams wrote down the context of each find. That means where it was in the ground, and what was near it. People lived at Ban Chiang. People were buried there too. The layers were not always neat. A pot from a grave makes us ask different questions.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: In 1974 and 1975, a team from Thailand and the United States dug at Ban Chiang. Careful digging like this is called excavation. The team noted the context of each find: where it was in the ground and what was near it. People once lived at Ban Chiang, and people were buried there too. The soil layers are not always neat. A pot from a grave makes us ask different questions.

read.sections.2.text.source: The second picture is a photo of one pot in a museum at Ban Chiang, taken in 2013. Start with observations: things you can see, such as its shape and its painted swirls. Then make an inference: an idea that might explain what you see. For example, someone chose to decorate this pot, because the pattern is there. But the photo cannot tell us who made the pot or which layer it came from. A museum label or an excavation record could help. When new evidence appears, historians change their ideas. Even the dates for Ban Chiang have changed over time.
read.sections.2.text.note: observation = สิ่งที่สังเกตเห็น and inference = ข้อสันนิษฐาน from KEY_TERMS (both marked check there). 'painted swirls' = ลายก้นหอยเขียนสี, the usual description of Ban Chiang painted pottery.
read.sections.2.text.back: The second picture is a photo of one pot in the museum at Ban Chiang, taken in 2013. Start with observations: what you can see, such as the pot's shape and the painted spiral pattern. Then make an inference: an idea that might explain what you see. For example: someone chose to decorate this pot, because there is a pattern on it. But the photo cannot tell who made this pot or which soil layer it came from. A museum label or excavation records might help. When there is new evidence, historians change their ideas. Even the age of Ban Chiang has changed over time.

watch.summary.source: This is a short film by UNESCO and NHK, a Japanese broadcaster. It is about the Ban Chiang site in northeast Thailand. UNESCO's description of the film makes some big claims. It says the site has the earliest evidence in the region of farming. It says the site also has the earliest evidence of making and using metal. Think about these claims as you watch. Words like "earliest" are claims, not observations. They depend on the evidence found so far. Researchers have changed the dates for Ban Chiang over time. So a careful viewer asks two questions. What evidence supports each claim? Could new evidence change it?
watch.summary.note: 'earliest' = เก่าแก่ที่สุด. Ban Chiang is a Thai national heritage site and the 'earliest' claim is a point of national pride; the Thai keeps the English framing (a claim, not an observation) exactly. A Thai reviewer should confirm it does not read as dismissive.
watch.summary.back: This is a short film by UNESCO and NHK, a Japanese television station, about the Ban Chiang site in north-eastern Thailand. UNESCO's description of the film makes some big claims. It says the site has the oldest evidence of farming in the region, and says it has the oldest evidence of making and using metal too. Think about these claims while you watch. Words like "oldest" are claims, not observations. They depend on the evidence found so far. Over time, researchers have changed the dates of Ban Chiang. So a careful viewer asks two questions. What evidence supports each claim? Could new evidence change that claim?

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Ban Chiang was a burial place as well as a village. The lesson names graves plainly and shows no human remains; keep discussion on objects and context, and preview the film for burials. sensitiveNotes.0.back: Ban Chiang is both a burial place and a village. The lesson talks about graves directly and does not show human remains. educatorNotes.0.source: Aim: learners separate an observation from a careful inference about one artefact, and say what its context could add. Evidence move: ask what the museum photo leaves out about the pot's excavation context (its layer, what lay near it, grave or house area). educatorNotes.1.source: Misconception to address: a museum display photo is not a photo of the object where it was found, and neither "all pots were for burial" nor "this pot belonged to a farmer" follows from it. Source caveats: avoid any "first ever" date; UNESCO says the site's dating has been adjusted as radiometric dating improved, and the 1995 Penn article (which the Penn Museum flags as a historical reference) gives older date ranges, so the lesson says only "more than 2,000 years ago". The photo is an example; nothing says which trench this pot came from.
